items.text: United Fidelity Bank of Evansville, Ind., was shut down by federal regulators Friday, the biggest U.S. bank failure in more than two years; depositors are protected.
items.detail: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency closed the $5.9 billion-asset lender, saying it was in an "unsafe or unsound condition," and named the FDIC receiver. First Citizens Bank of Raleigh, N.C., agreed to take over substantially all deposits and assets, so customers keep their money and insurance coverage without doing anything; United Fidelity's 22 branches in Indiana, Illinois, Florida, Colorado and the U.S. Virgin Islands reopen as First Citizens branches Saturday or Monday. The FDIC estimates the failure will cost its Deposit Insurance Fund $1.83 billion. It is the largest failure since Philadelphia's Republic First Bank closed in April 2024 with about $6 billion in assets, Reuters reported.
items.why: A multibillion-dollar bank failure tests the deposit-insurance fund and draws attention to strains in regional lenders.

items.text: An explosion at a school in Afghanistan's Kunar province killed seven people and wounded more than 90 Saturday morning, a provincial official said.
items.detail: Sami ul Haq Bayan, Kunar's culture and information director, said the 10 a.m. blast on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, appeared to start in a neighboring depot storing explosives for mining companies and that early information pointed to negligence there; an investigation is underway. Up to 15 of the wounded remained in the hospital. Part of the school building appeared to collapse.
items.why: Children were among the victims of a blast officials tie to poorly guarded mining explosives.

items.text: The Army's detonation of degraded lead azide in Iowa did not raise lead in drinking-water sources, the EPA said in its first post-blast lab results.
items.detail: EPA found no lead in 38 water samples taken after Wednesday's blast at public water supplies, both treated and untreated. Air monitors had read zero airborne lead for 30 straight hours. The agency has collected more than 3,200 air, water, soil and dust samples and has resampled 88% of homes tested beforehand; results for tap water, soil and dust will be posted at epa.gov/IowaData as they are validated.
items.why: Nearby residents in Iowa, Illinois and Missouri had feared lead fallout from the detonation.

items.text: Iran's claims that its navy retook two tankers seized by U.S. forces and once struck the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln are false, U.S. Central Command said.
items.detail: Iranian navy commander Shahram Irani had said, according to Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, that Iranian forces boarded two oil tankers "stolen" by the U.S. while American troops slept, and Tehran also said the U.S. charges ships $2.5 million to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. CENTCOM called the tanker account "another fabricated lie," said "Iran no longer has a navy," said the Lincoln strike group was never hit and returned home last month, and said there is no toll for ships in the strait. Neither side's claims could be independently verified. The exchange came a day after CENTCOM said it disabled the cargo ship Pacific Archer for trying to run the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports.
items.why: Dueling claims over the Strait of Hormuz show how tense the standoff at sea remains as Iran vows to break the U.S. blockade.

items.text: The S&P 500 rose 1.6% in Friday's shortened post-Thanksgiving session, finishing its best week since April 2025 with a 5.6% gain.
items.detail: The S&P 500 closed at 7,297.49, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points (1.2%) to 50,774.94, and the Nasdaq composite rose 2.3% to 24,129.50. For the week the S&P 500 gained 5.6%, the Dow 5.5% and the Nasdaq 6.7%, a sharp turnaround from the prior week, when the S&P 500 finished more than 10% below last month's record high. Technology stocks led again, but about 4 of every 5 stocks in the index rose. Markets closed early at 1 p.m. ET after being shut Thursday for Thanksgiving.
items.why: The rebound erases much of the recent correction that hit retirement and investment accounts.

items.text: The U.S. military disabled a cargo ship that tried to run its blockade of Iranian ports, striking the Pacific Archer's stern from the air, Central Command said Friday.
items.detail: CENTCOM said a U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the Palau-flagged bulk carrier M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after the ship left Iran's Bandar Abbas port and ignored multiple warnings; its propulsion was disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed. Ship-tracking sites listed its destination as Singapore, AP reported. CENTCOM said U.S. forces have redirected 158 compliant commercial ships and disabled six that refused during the blockade, which resumed in mid-July. Iran's navy chief, Rear Adm. Shahram Irani, said on state TV that Iran will carry out operations to break the blockade, and Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, said the Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened. The war reaches nine months on Saturday.
items.why: Each forced stop raises the risk of a direct clash at sea as Iran vows to break the blockade, keeping Gulf shipping and oil prices on edge.

items.text: Quebec's Bill 21, which bars many public workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, was largely upheld Friday by the Supreme Court of Canada.
items.detail: In English Montreal School Board v. Quebec (2026 SCC 41), the court ruled Quebec validly used the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the 2019 secularism law, reaffirming its 1988 Ford ruling that the override has no limits beyond its text; six of the seven judges joined that holding. The one part struck down: the face-covering rule cannot apply to elected members of Quebec's National Assembly, which violates the Charter right to seek office and sit as a legislator. The court said judges may still declare a law inconsistent with the Charter despite the override, but four of the seven declined to do so here; Justices Karakatsanis, Kasirer and O'Bonsawin wrote that the law infringes religious freedom, expression and equality. Challenges brought by Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers and the English Montreal School Board were dismissed. Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study the ruling.
items.why: The ruling confirms provinces can override Charter rights with few limits, keeping hijab-, turban- and cross-wearing teachers and officials out of many Quebec public jobs.

items.text: China's stock markets jumped Friday, the Shanghai index rising 3.73%, after the State Council promised more state-fund buying to steady prices.
items.detail: The Shanghai Composite closed up 3.73% at 3,606.49, back above 3,600; the Shenzhen Component rose 7.24% to 10,814.02, the ChiNext board 11.61% and the STAR Composite 14.21%, Xinhua reported. Chip and electronics stocks led and banks lagged. A State Council executive meeting Friday called for stronger market-stabilizing mechanisms, more dividends and buybacks from listed companies, a bigger role for state-backed funds including Central Huijin Investment as a quasi-"stabilization fund," and steering insurance, annuity and social-security money into stocks. Reuters said it was the biggest daily gain since the October 2024 stimulus, after the market had fallen to 16-month lows. Separately, the National Bureau of Statistics said Friday that industrial profits rose 20.1% in October from a year earlier, and 16.0% in January-October.
items.why: It is Beijing's most direct move yet to stop a slide in the world's No. 2 stock market as tariff threats and the AI-stock sell-off weigh on markets.

week.text: Inflation rose to 3.8% in October by the Fed's preferred gauge, nearly double its 2% goal, the Commerce Department said Wednesday.
week.detail: The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.3% from September and 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 3.3% from a year ago. Personal income jumped 0.7% and spending rose 0.3%; the saving rate was 4.1%. A separate Commerce report revised third-quarter growth up to a 4.3% annual rate, the fastest in three years. Markets fully price a quarter-point Fed rate hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. Jobless claims fell to 189,000, near the lowest since the late 1960s.
week.why: Hotter inflation with a strong economy makes a December rate hike, and higher borrowing costs, very likely.

week.text: Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO and president Monday, effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned; the company's shares jumped about 31%.
week.detail: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring Huang back, and to his board seat, after meetings in which it said it was satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead." The board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government" and is confident his return "poses no national security risk." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials suspected of working for Chinese intelligence; board chair Harvey Jones said on the Nov. 17 earnings call that the board did not intend to reinstate him. President Trump called it "the correct and proper decision" on Truth Social and said the attorney general has no evidence Huang broke the law. Colette Kress, interim CEO since Nov. 12, returns to her finance role. Nvidia closed up about 31.5%, its best day since 2000, adding roughly $900 billion in market value.
week.why: The return of the head of the world's most valuable chipmaker, with the government's blessing, reset the AI trade that dragged stocks into a correction last week.

week.text: The Thanksgiving storm's power outages peaked near 1 million U.S. homes and businesses Thursday night, up from 600,000 that afternoon; more than 800,000 were still out early Friday.
week.detail: More than 961,000 customers were without power at 7:30 p.m. ET Thursday, according to PowerOutage.us data cited by Reuters, including more than 235,000 in Pennsylvania, 180,000 in New Jersey, 156,000 in Maryland, 132,000 in Virginia and about 106,000 in Missouri. More than 800,000 were still out as of about 12:30 a.m. Friday, AP reported. FlightAware counted more than 460 U.S. flight cancellations and more than 2,500 delays Thursday. Avalon, N.J., saw one of the worst floods in its history ("Not quite Hurricane Sandy," an official said), and U.S. Route 30 into Atlantic City closed. The Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission asked all 1.9 million customers to conserve water because outages threatened its two filtration plants. St. Louis got 7.3 inches of snow and Ste. Genevieve, Mo., 14 inches; the roof of an empty ice arena collapsed in Wentzville, Mo. All of New Jersey and parts of New York remain under states of emergency. The National Weather Service expected conditions to improve, with gusts of 25-35 mph Friday.
week.why: Hundreds of thousands are still without power as people travel home from the holiday.
